negative_findings.finding: Investigated whether specific Southern counties/towns can be tied to specific Chicago neighborhoods as chain-migration feeders. Found strong state-level and city-level patterns (Mississippi Delta towns - Clarksdale/Stovall, Winona, Vicksburg, Chickasaw County; Alabama - Montgomery, Tuscaloosa, Birmingham; Georgia; Louisiana - New Orleans - all feeding Chicago's South Side/Bronzeville), documented family by family. Did NOT locate an archivally or statistically demonstrated feeder-county-to-named-neighborhood chain (e.g., 'Holmes County, MS to West Woodlawn') in this pass.

Broad reverse-migration statistics are documented (Frey/Brookings 2004: Chicago among metros with substantial Black outmigration in the late 1990s while Atlanta and other Southern metros gained; Stack's Call to Home documents returns to nine Carolina counties but uses pseudonyms and is not Chicago-specific). Only two named individuals with a Chicago-to-South return were documented in this pass: Margaret Walker (Chicago to Jackson State College, MS, 1949) and Sun Ra (Chicago to Birmingham, 1990-93, for family care after a stroke). No widely documented working-class Chicago returnee was found.

Investigated direct institutional links between Chicago and Detroit Black cultural institutions (e.g., Motown-Chicago label partnerships). Found meaningful bilateral traces - the Nation of Islam's 1934 headquarters move (Detroit to Chicago), John Lee Hooker's Detroit-to-Chicago recording relationship with Vee-Jay, and Detroit's Funk Brothers playing on Hooker's 1961 Chicago 'Boom Boom' session - but no documented formal partnership or joint institution. Motown itself shows no Chicago institutional footprint in sources consulted.

Documented: Langston Hughes's decades-long Chicago Defender column (Harlem writer to Chicago paper, from Feb 1943); the UNIA's Harlem headquarters to Chicago division pipeline (Garvey's Sept 1919 visit); the BSCP's New York leadership to Chicago division. NOT found: a formal Harlem-Chicago civic-institutional compact (e.g., linked churches, schools, or municipal programs). The Chitlin' Circuit venue network (including Chicago's Regal and Harlem's Apollo) is frequently asserted as a linkage but was not verified with a citable source in this pass.

The evidence assembled supports discrete bilateral corridors and hub-and-spoke networks (Mississippi Delta-Chicago via Illinois Central; New Orleans-Chicago jazz; Memphis-Chicago blues recording pipeline; Atlanta-Chicago civil-rights axis; Harlem-Chicago press/movement links; Detroit-Chicago via NOI and studio sessions), NOT a single integrated 'world system.' The closest multi-node systems are the Black press wire network (Defender + ANP correspondents in every major Black population center) and the Pullman porter information network. The track should avoid imposing a world-system model where evidence shows bilateral links.

The claim that Jelly Roll Morton moved from New Orleans to Chicago in 1923 is widely repeated but was not verified with an archival or scholarly source in this pass; omitted from entities pending verification.

This is a negative finding, not evidence of an exchange.

negative_findings.finding: Hill 60 'Chicago Steelband' (Trinidad) is a naming false positive.

The Consulate General of Haiti estimated ~40,000 self-reported Haitians in Chicago (TRiiBE, 2026) — a consular estimate, not Census/ACS data. Use neither as a verified count.

The YMCA's role as the ASNLH's 1915 founding venue is documented; 'first YMCA in the Midwest to serve people of color' alone is not a documented intercity relationship.

Evidence supports several bilateral or hub-and-spoke networks centered on Chicago (Defender distribution, ANP correspondents, headquarters relocations, convention hosting, delegation trips) but not a single integrated world system. The dataset should not be read as one.
